YouTube use includes adults' videos watched by children, not only content labeled Made for Kids
Study uses regulator aggregate statistics only; no child-level watch history, identities or sensitive attributes

limitations: The 2024–2025 percentage change is year-over-year, not seasonal lift within either year.
TV-set share and total in-home minutes use compatible age and device scopes but measure different units; do not multiply them into unique viewers.
Barb in-home broadband viewing excludes some out-of-home and cellular traffic, so not the full viewing population.
Children's viewing time is not synonymous with Made for Kids content, preschool viewing or educational content.
Shorts, live and copyright-audio-matched selected channel audiences may be excluded from some provider-specific panels.
Child location, gender, interests, profiles, watch histories and credentials must not be collected for this research.
UK measures cannot be projected onto all countries without appropriate independent frames.
The U.S. Nielsen May-to-June 2025 changes are TV impressions for ages 6–17 across all sources or all streaming; neither is the change in YouTube child viewers or viewing minutes.
Month-on-month TV increases at the beginning of summer are not causal estimates of school breaks, nor UK seasonality or made-for-kids video demand.
Nielsen's August 2025 declines are for TV-screen viewing among ages 6–17, not YouTube-only viewing, uniquely identified children, content genres or creator earnings.
Nielsen's five-week viewing interval does not isolate back-to-school causality, and a May–June impressions change cannot be compounded with July–August viewing-time change.

adjacent_seasonal_context.context: TV-screen usage as schools let out, not a YouTube-specific viewing series

adjacent_school_return_context.target_population: Nielsen-measured television-screen viewing among school-aged children and teens
adjacent_school_return_context.methodological_boundary: Same measurement system and broad age cohort as Nielsen June article, but the May–June report concerns TV impressions, whereas August concerns viewing time and streaming usage in a different window; percentages must not be chained to construct YouTube seasonal change.
